opening.headline: Whether AI costs increase proportionally to the number of people or usage depends on the charging method.
body: If AI is opened to all employees, will the cost increase in proportion to the number of people? If AI is added to the customer inquiry system, will the cost increase as the number of inquiries increases? The billing methods for the two cases are different. If you don't know the difference, you'll end up using the wrong numbers when setting your budget.

In this class, we will look side by side at subscription-type charging, where each person pays a flat fee, and token charging, which adds up input and output tokens according to the amount spent. We compare the cost-increasing structures of the two methods and apply them to two cases: a tool for a small number of experts and an enterprise-wide customer response system to determine which is correct.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the difference between subscription-type charging and token charging
You can distinguish between charging methods that fit your work patterns.

screens.title: Does the cost increase with the number of people or with the amount of usage?
screens.lead: Read the two introductory scenes and predict how the costs will increase for each.

visual.alt: A picture showing the scene of opening AI to all employees and the scene of adding AI to the customer inquiry system, side by side.
labels: Adding AI to the customer inquiry system

paragraphs: This is the first scene. The company has decided to open AI to all employees. As the number of employees increases, costs are likely to increase accordingly. The budget is based on how much it costs per person.

This is the second scene. AI responses have been added to customer inquiry channels. This time, customers are the users, not employees, and there is a big difference between days when there is a lot of inquiries and days when there is a lot of inquiries. It seems that the cost will increase as the number of inquiries increases, but it is not easy to guess how much it will increase.

The two scenes are billed differently. One side is a flat rate per person, and the other side is a sum of usage units. This class explains the difference by dividing it into subscription type and token charging.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: How does the method of creating a budget differ depending on whether the unit that creates the cost is a person or a request?

screens.outro: Let’s start by recalling a familiar method.

screens.title: Personal subscription or API usage billing: which one are you more familiar with?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: Is the cost the same for monthly services no matter how many times I use them?
items.answer: The rates are the same, but often not unlimited. AI subscription plans also have usage limits for each plan. If you exceed the limit, you will have to wait or upgrade to a higher plan.

items.prompt: Have you ever used a service where you are billed based on the amount you spend?
items.answer: The same goes for electricity bills or cloud usage fees. Low usage months are cheap and high usage months are expensive. API charging also has this structure, and the unit of usage is a token.

items.prompt: Which costs are easier to predict?
items.answer: If you have a set number of people, the subscription type is easier to predict. If usage changes significantly over time, token charges are difficult to predict, but since you only pay for what you use, there is less waste. Rather than saying which one is better, it is more accurate to say that there is one that fits your work pattern.

screens.outro: Let's look at both methods in turn. First of all, it is a subscription type.

screens.title: Subscription-type billing: Flat rate per person, limit based on usage
screens.lead: Move the slider to change the plan stage. As you move up the tiers, you can see how the usage and features included change.

visual.alt: An illustration showing the usage limit bar getting longer as the plan level increases.
labels: Total subscription cost = Number of subscribers × Plan unit price
If you exceed the limit, wait or go to a higher plan

stops.body: This is the first step in Claude's pricing guide. Chat for free on the web, desktop, and mobile, and enjoy features like web browsing, file creation, code execution, and app linking. Google AI also has a Free stage. Even if it is free, usage limits apply.

Claude Pro includes Free plus more usage and features like Claude Code and Projects. The fee is $17 per month if paid on a yearly basis, and $20 if paid on a monthly basis. Google AI tells us that Plus offers usage limits that are twice as high as Free, and Pro offers four times higher usage limits. As you move up, limits, models, and feature access increase.

Claude Max comes in your choice of 5x or 20x the usage of Pro. It starts at $100 per month and includes higher power limits and priority access during peak hours on all jobs. It's aimed at people who work with AI all day.

Choosing a higher tier will result in larger usage limits. Google AI Ultra will also be ushered in with 5x or 20x higher limits compared to AI Pro. However, usage limits apply at any stage, so a flat rate is not unlimited. If you exceed the limit, you will have to wait or get a higher plan.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the subscription structure, let’s look at token charging based on usage.

screens.title: Token charging: As input and output are used
screens.lead: Select each tab to learn how token charges are calculated and how the unit price varies depending on the model.

tabs.label: basic structure
tabs.body: The API is billed based on the amount of tokens used. A token is the unit by which the model processes text. The price list displays input and output prices separately based on MTok, which usually means 1 million tokens. The tokens sent as input and tokens received as output are counted and added up.

tabs.label: Claude model unit price
tabs.body: The Claude model overview shows input and output unit costs for each model separately. Fable 5.1 costs $10 per million tokens input and $50 per million tokens output. The Opus 5.5 is $4 and $20, the Sonnet 5.5 is $2 and $10, and the Haiku 5.5 starts at $0.10 for input and $0.50 for output. Even within the same company, unit prices can vary by more than 100 times depending on the model.

tabs.label: OpenAI model unit price
tabs.body: The OpenAI model document also provides separate input and output costs for each model. The most powerful GPT-6 Astra costs $10 for input and $50 for output. The balanced GPT-6.1 Sol has an input of $2 and an output of $10, while the cost-sensitive, high-volume GPT-6 Luna has an input of $0.1 and an output of $0.5. The documentation tells you to choose between these three models depending on your intended use.

tabs.label: Meaning of output unit price
tabs.body: In all three documents, the output unit price is displayed higher than the input unit price. So the more long answers you create, the more expensive it becomes. The Gemini API document also introduces models divided by purpose, so choosing between a heavy model and a light model according to the nature of the work is the key to cost management.

screens.outro: Now that we have confirmed the structure of the two methods, let us compare the structure of increasing costs at a glance.

screens.title: Structure of increasing costs at a glance
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the total cost increases under subscription type and token charging.

states.label: Subscription type
states.body: The total cost increases by the number of subscribers multiplied by the plan price. If you add one more person, the cost increases by the set unit price, and the bill is the same regardless of whether one person uses a lot or a little. Usage is controlled by limits, not amounts. For those who only spend within the limit, the subscription plan is easier to predict, and if you frequently reach your limit, you should consider a higher plan.

states.label: Token charging
states.body: The total cost is the number of requests multiplied by the token length per request and the model unit price, adding up inputs and outputs separately. For example, let's calculate it using the unit price of a document. If there are 10,000 requests and the input is 2,000 tokens and the output is 500 tokens per request, then the input is 20 million tokens and the output is 5 million tokens. The Sonnet 5.5 unit price is $90, including $40 for input and $50 for output. The same request, calculated at the starting price of Haiku 5.5, is $4.50 ($2 for input plus $2.50 for output). Switching to a smaller model will lower the unit price, and as requests increase, costs will increase proportionally. You can do this calculation yourself using a price table, so it's a good idea to estimate the cost range before adoption, assuming the expected number and length of requests.

screens.outro: Now let's apply the structure to an example. First, it is a tool for a few professionals.

screens.title: Commentary: Tools for Minorities
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step what charging is appropriate for the tools used by eight analysts. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Check the situation
steps.body: Eight analysts use AI to analyze and draft documents all day long. There are a limited number of users, and each person's usage is large. In this pattern, both number of people and usage affect costs.

steps.title: Step 1 Usage Pattern
steps.body: There are a fixed number of users and each person has a large usage volume. However, it is difficult to predict in advance how much one person will spend per day and the upper limit. The first clue is that the unit that creates the cost is more of a person than a request.

steps.title: 2-level subscription type
steps.body: Since the number of people is fixed, monthly costs are easy to predict. You can talk as much as you like within limits, and each analyst's bill is the same even in the months when they spend the most. The advantage is that it is easy to create and explain a budget.

steps.title: Step 3 Token charging
steps.body: As each analyst frequently enters long documents, input tokens accumulate. If you have a large input per entry, your bill at the end of the month can change significantly. If you have a lot of users, it may be more expensive than a subscription plan.

steps.title: Step 4 Judgment
steps.body: For a small number of regular users, subscriptions are more predictable. However, we need to check whether analysts hit their limits frequently. If you reach frequently, consider whether you need a higher plan.

steps.title: Instructor's Summary
steps.body: The key to this example is that there are a limited number of users, and they are all people. In these cases, start with a subscription plan with easier-to-predict costs and adjust your plan based on how often you reach your limits. Conversely, if the tools used by analysts are built into the system and changed to be called automatically, then token charging must be reexamined.

screens.outro: This time, we will look at a company-wide customer service system with the opposite structure.

screens.title: Commentary: Company-wide customer service system
screens.lead: The instructor explains step by step what charging is appropriate for the inquiry channel used by tens of thousands of customers. Select the right arrow to see the steps.

steps.title: Check the situation
steps.body: We are trying to attach AI responses to customer inquiry channels. We have tens of thousands of customers. Users are customers, not employees, and inquiry volume varies greatly depending on the time of day and season.

steps.title: Step 1 Usage Pattern
steps.body: It is not the person who creates the cost, but each inquiry. There is a big difference in usage between days when there are a lot of inquiries and quiet days. If you budget based on the number of people, it won't work.

steps.title: Limitations of 2-level subscription type
steps.body: You can't give each customer a subscription. It is also difficult to express how the system calls the model with a per-person fixed amount. The subscription type is suitable for cases where people use it directly on the screen.

steps.title: Step 3 Token charging
steps.body: Costs increase proportionally to the number of inquiries and length of response. Costs also rise in months when there is a high volume of inquiries. Instead, in months when there are fewer inquiries, you are billed only for what you use, eliminating waste, and any changes in usage are directly reflected in your costs.

steps.title: 4-step cost management
steps.body: API token charging fits into the structure. Unit costs can be managed by dividing simple classifications into low-cost models and complex inquiries into higher-cost models. Since the output cost is high, it may also be beneficial to shorten unnecessarily long answers. If you calculate your monthly cost range in advance, assuming a peak season for inquiries, you can avoid exceeding your budget.

steps.title: Comparison of the two cases
steps.body: The reason the charging structures in the two cases are different is because the unit that creates the cost is different, whether it is a person or a request. A small number of fixed users tend to be eligible for subscription pricing, while those with fluctuating requests, such as from external customers or system calls, tend to be eligible for token charging.

screens.outro: Now that we've solved the two cases, let's summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key Takeaway: Subscriptions are proportional to number of people, tokens are proportional to usage
screens.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class. Read while remembering the question asked at the beginning: what is the unit that creates the cost?

paragraphs: Subscription charging costs increase in proportion to the number of people, and token charging increases in proportion to the number and length of requests and model unit price. The subscription type also has usage limits for each plan, so the flat rate is not unlimited. Token charging counts input and output separately, and the output unit price tends to be displayed higher.

The unit price of the model varies greatly depending on the purpose, so the cost depends on which model you use. So, when choosing a charging method, we first consider whether the unit that creates the cost is a person or a request. The subscription type tends to be appropriate for a small number of users who consistently use within the limit, while token charging tends to be appropriate for cases where usage fluctuates significantly and system calls are made.

Even though each company's rate guide has a similar structure, the units and terminology are different, so you need to get into the habit of translating them into the same framework and comparing them.

callout.label: standards to remember
callout.text: Subscriptions are proportional to the number of people and tokens are proportional to usage. Check the unit that creates the cost.

glossary.def: Each user pays a set monthly fee and spends within the limits of each plan.
This is a method of charging the model unit price according to the amount of input and output tokens.
This is the upper limit on the amount you can spend in a certain period of time on a subscription plan.
This unit represents 1 million tokens and is the basis for the model price list.
This is the amount of tokens the model can handle at one time.

misconceptions.myth: If you have a flat subscription, you can use it as much as you want.
misconceptions.fact: Each plan has usage limits. If you exceed the limit, you will have to wait or get a higher plan.

misconceptions.myth: Token charging is always cheaper than subscription.
misconceptions.fact: If your usage is large and consistent, token charges may be more expensive. Which one is cheaper depends on your usage patterns.

misconceptions.myth: Models from the same company have the same unit price.
misconceptions.fact: Input and output unit costs vary greatly between models. In both Claude and OpenAI documents, the unit cost of the most powerful model and the model for mass processing differs by more than dozens of times.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Subscription costs increase in proportion to the number of people and token costs increase in proportion to usage.
Subscriptions also have limits, and token charging counts input and output separately.
Model cost varies greatly depending on the intended use, and model selection determines cost.
Choose a billing unit that fits your work pattern.
